It appears that the universal nostalgia for everything 2000s-coded is not slowing down as we move further into the second half of 2026, and the owners of one of the most iconic online platforms of that era are now reportedly looking to cash in. Speaking in a recent documentary called “Myspace,” the cofounders of Viant Technology — the company that bought Myspace alongside Justin Timberlake in 2011 , when it was trading as Specific Media — confirmed : “We are stewards of the Myspace brand at this point, and we are going to relaunch Myspace. We’re just waiting for the right time to do it.” They later added, somewhat pessimistically, “And if that one doesn’t work, we’ll do it again.” Clearly the travails of trying to recapture the initial buzz of a social media platform, especially one that came to dominate the online culture early on, aren’t lost on the current Myspace owners. Given the relatively limited hype cycle of social media platforms, the Viant chiefs are probably right to be hesitant about bringing Myspace back kicking and screaming into 2026, when the market is almost as crowded as ever. The fact that, by their own admission , they burned about $150 million on trying to redesign the site with more of a music focus in 2013 is probably also in their minds when mulling the decision to bide their time a little. Although millennial Myspace enthusiasts have greeted the potential relaunch news with glee, it’s difficult to imagine a platform that peaked around 20 years ago making a splash in any truly meaningful way, even if it would offer a more authentic Y2K-tinged alternative to some of the sanitized platforms that have come to loom large in the social media landscape of 2026. title: 💊 Novo pops a pill

Stocks finished strong on Friday capping off a week for the books, with the S&P 500 finishing up 0.6% on the day and up 3.6% over the week. Is Novo Nordisk’s ’s losing streak coming to an end? Novo is getting a boost from its Wegovy pill , which has been flying off the pharmacy shelves since it came to market in January. In the first quarter of this year, sales for the drug were nearly twice what Wall Street was penciling in. It’s been the biggest GLP-1 debut by volume ever. According to Novo, the pill has now reached over 5 million total prescriptions and it's only accelerating: it took 12 weeks to reach its first 1 million patients, but its latest 1 million were added in just a month. A big chunk of that has been through its direct-to-consumer platform. “We are more and more ourselves getting surprised [by] how many people are after a pill rather than an injection, frankly,” CEO Mike Doustdar told analysts on August 5. It’s a bright spot in an otherwise gloomy picture for the Danish pharmaceutical company. Novo has increasingly lost ground to its rival , Eli Lilly, in the lucrative injectable weight loss and diabetes drug market, which still accounts for the vast majority of GLP-1 prescriptions. Eli Lilly — despite having the best-selling drug in the world, Mounjaro and Zepbound — has had an underwhelming debut for its weight loss pill, Foundayo. The drug, which came to market in April, brought in $98 million in revenue in the second quarter, less than the $103 million the Street was expecting. While its pill may not be a blockbuster (yet, at least), the company’s next-generation injectable drug, retatrutide, has had impressive results in clinical trials. So impressive many people aren’t even waiting for FDA approval to start taking it. It’s worth noting that all signs suggest the introduction of oral GLP-1 options has expanded the population of patients on these drugs, meaning they likely aren’t taking away sales from injectables already on the market. While Novo was early to the GLP-1 market with Ozempic, it has spent the past year or so living under Lilly’s shadow. The Wegovy pill has certainly changed the vibe for Novo. Brian Mulberry, chief market strategist at Zacks Investment Management, which holds both Lilly and Novo, said the biggest question is if Novo will be able to get the pill to as many patients who want it. The company has had issues with manufacturing capacity in the past. “That all comes down to execution though, and Novo has seen headwinds in ramping up scale to compete with their larger peers,” Mulberry said. The pickup truck has fundamentally shifted in American car culture. Once an effective workhorse primarily marketed to businesses and trades for its utility, the trucks have mutated, from hyper-functional, stripped down vehicles to aspirational purchases priced at levels attainable only for the upper middle class, stuffed with sophisticated technology and creature comforts. That’s what people are buying, so that’s what automakers are selling. That said, a growing set of evidence indicates that this auto niche is leaving behind a lot of possible customers. This thesis has been borne out in a number of emerging competitors to the flagship Ford pickup truck, the F-150, including but not limited to: Chinese automobiles, mostly electric, that have been driving circles around American autos overseas. Stateside competition from the likes of Slate Auto , the Jeff Bezos-backed startup that has promised a $25,000 customizable electric pickup, which is premised on the observation that cars are mostly built today for the top 30% of the market , and is instead choosing to target the other 70%. Tesla , which has its own direct competitor in the oversized and expensive status symbol pickup truck segment in the Cybertruck. Ford’s first attempt to address some of these competitors, the F-150 Lightning, missed the mark and led to a $19.5 billion charge in December . Beset on all sides, Ford’s not going to have a lot more chances to win. That’s one reason the company has been preparing the Universal Electric Vehicle platform , which will allow the company to build EVs more efficiently on the same production lines, in a strategic shift that the company describes as essentially turning the assembly line into an “assembly tree.” Ford has announced the first vehicle built on that platform will be its new electric pickup truck, dubbed the Fathom , that will hit the market starting at $28,350. That list price is nearly half the cost of the average US sales price of a new vehicle in June, and is only slightly more expensive than the average used car. This comes at a financial inflection point for the automobile business in general and the EV business in particular. Used EV prices have been increasing in 2026, defying the gravity that usually hangs on used car prices amid high gasoline prices from the Iran war. The sticker shock from high auto prices has had some significant reverberations around the economy as well; the average MSRP of a new vehicle in June 2026 was $51,394 . With interest rates still well above their post-pandemic lows, car loan terms that were once unthinkable — well past the standard four years, stretching even as high as eight years — have become downright common . That’s why the sub-$30,000 price point is so compelling: Ford’s either got to find a way to sell cars to the middle class again, or the likes of China and Slate Auto are going to do it for them.
